answer.decision: Start signing with the new key immediately while temporarily verifying tokens with both the old and new public keys.
answer.action: Distribute the new public key to every verifying service, disable the old private key for signing, and activate new-key signing as one coordinated change. Continue accepting the old public key for at least the 45-minute access-token lifetime plus a small clock-skew and in-flight-request buffer, while remaining well below the 24-hour policy limit. Monitor token rejections and service key-loading status, then remove the old verification key once no legitimately issued old-key access tokens can remain valid.
reasons: This is the only option that immediately stops old-key signing without invalidating all outstanding old-key access tokens.
Access tokens expire after 45 minutes, while server-side refresh validation allows subsequent access tokens to be issued under the new key.
All deployed services support two verification keys without restarting, making a coordinated dual-verification window feasible.
Legacy client age does not require old-key signing because clients rely on server-published keys rather than embedded signing keys.
New-key-only verification could force active users with outstanding tokens to reauthenticate and jeopardize the 2 percent forced-logout limit.
Continuing old-key signing until legacy clients update directly violates the immediate-stop constraint.
assumptions: The new public key can be loaded by all token-verifying services before or atomically with the switch to new-key signing.
No access token remains valid beyond its stated 45-minute lifetime except for a bounded allowance for clock skew and in-flight requests.
Refresh-token validation and issuance can produce new-key access tokens without requiring client updates.
Monitoring can identify key-distribution failures and old-key token rejections during the overlap.
risks: If any verifier has not loaded the new public key when signing switches, it may reject newly issued tokens.
Removing old-key verification too early could reject legitimately issued tokens and force logouts.
Keeping old-key verification active allows forged tokens from a compromised old private key to be accepted during the overlap, so the window should be minimized.
Clock skew, issuance timing, caching, or inconsistent service configuration could require a slightly longer overlap than exactly 45 minutes.
A service that fails to remove the old public key after the planned window could unintentionally extend exposure.

citations.claim: The strategy must keep forced logout below 2 percent, stop old-key signing immediately, and may temporarily retain old-key verification.
Access tokens expire after 45 minutes, and refresh tokens are validated server-side.
All deployed services can load two verification keys without restarting.
Security policy permits verification-key overlap for no more than 24 hours.
Old-key signing can be disabled independently of retaining its public verification material.
Clients rely on services using server-published public keys rather than embedding signing keys.
